## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

1. **Verify, do not assume.** After every restore step, check the result with `ls`, `du`,
   or a file count. A command that exits 0 can still have done nothing.
2. **Never delete anything on the backup drive.** It is the only copy present on this
   machine. No `rm`, no `mv` off the drive, no reformatting. Copy *from* it only.
3. **Stop at CHECKPOINTs.** Show the user what you found and wait. Do not batch through.
4. **Two failures = stop and ask.** If a step fails twice, do not try a third approach.
   Report what happened and wait for direction.
5. **Never invent a credential.** If a step needs an API key you do not have, say so and
   move on. A placeholder value is worse than a missing file — it fails confusingly later.
6. **Expect this document to be wrong somewhere.** It was written on 2026-08-04 on the old
   Windows machine and has never been executed. When reality disagrees with it, reality
   wins — record the discrepancy and tell the user at the end (Phase I).

```bash

export SSD="/Volumes/ASSISTANT/AssistantBackup"     # adjust if the name differs

cat "$SSD/MANIFEST/TRANSFER-CHECK.txt"

Expect these directories: `DEV-repo-data`, `DEV-nonrepo`, `DEV-working-tree`, `repos`,
`claude`, `codex`, `gemini`, `SecondBrain`, `MANIFEST`, `_receipts`.

## Phase 8 — Platform fixes

**Port the backup script.** `~/.claude/scripts/daily-backup.ps1` needs: `robocopy` →
`rsync -a` (no `--delete`; the store is deliberately additive), `Register-ScheduledTask` →
the plists above, and Windows paths → macOS paths.

**Do NOT point the nightly backup at the USB stick you restored from.** It is transport
only. Measured write throughput on 2026-08-04 was ~3 MB/s — a nightly run would take over
an hour, and flash wears out under exactly that pattern. Until a proper external SSD is
attached to this Mac, set `destinations.ssd.optional = true` and let the job warn that the
target is absent; the GitHub and Drive paths still run. When a real drive arrives, format
it exFAT, give it a label with no spaces, and set `destinations.ssd.root` to its
`/Volumes/<LABEL>/AssistantBackup` path.

Preserve these behaviours when porting — each was added to fix a real failure:
- **Default-deny.** A DEV directory absent from the manifest must raise an error.
- **Coverage computed, not assumed.** Capture uses `git ls-files --others --ignored` and
  `git diff --name-only` as authority, never a hand-written ignore regex.
- **The credential deny-list.** Files are gitignored for two opposite reasons — too big
  (back up) and secret (never). On 2026-08-04 the capture swept 7,633 files of a live
  authenticated Outlook browser profile onto a portable drive. Do not weaken this.
- **Receipts.** Write a sentinel to each destination and read it back.
- **Additive, never mirrored.** A mirror replicates the deletion you are recovering from.

**Depath the three Windows-bound files:** `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`,
`scripts/daily-backup.ps1`, `scripts/fix-msys-ad-stall.ps1`. `settings.json` and the hooks
are already portable. **Delete `fix-msys-ad-stall.ps1`** — same reasoning as MsysKeepAlive.

Rewrite the tool-path block in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` for macOS, and drop its
"prefer PowerShell over Bash" rule — that existed only because of the Windows Git-Bash
stall. On macOS, zsh/bash is the native surface.

upper bound and most are incidental. Confirmed work:

|---|---|---|

| `closeout`, `project-triage`, `forecast-capture` | call `.ps1` with Windows paths | path fixes; `pwsh` runs them |
| `html-to-pdf` | hardcoded Chrome path | `/Applications/Google Chrome.app/...` |

Triage the rest as you hit them. A broken skill is a nuisance, not data loss.

#!/bin/bash
# Repair Phase 4.1: clones failed (no network during restore). Folders in ~/DEV
# already hold overlay data (gitignored files + uncommitted edits). Strategy:
# init in place, fetch, point HEAD+index at origin's default branch, then check
# out ONLY tracked files that are missing. Never overwrite an existing file.
set -u
DEV="$HOME/DEV"
repair() {
  local dir="$1" remote="$2"
  local d="$DEV/$dir"
  mkdir -p "$d"
  if [ -d "$d/.git" ]; then echo "SKIP  $dir (already a git repo)"; return; fi
  cd "$d" || { echo "FAIL  $dir (cd)"; return; }
  git init -q || { echo "FAIL  $dir (init)"; return; }
  git remote add origin "https://github.com/$remote.git"
  if ! git fetch -q origin 2>/tmp/fetch.err; then
    echo "FAIL  $dir (fetch: $(head -1 /tmp/fetch.err))"
    rm -rf "$d/.git"
    return
  fi
  local db
  db=$(git ls-remote --symref origin HEAD 2>/dev/null | awk '/^ref: refs\/heads\// {sub("refs/heads/","",$2); print $2; exit}')
  [ -z "$db" ] && db=$(git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short)' refs/remotes/origin | grep -vE 'HEAD' | head -1 | sed 's|origin/||')
  if [ -z "$db" ]; then echo "FAIL  $dir (no default branch)"; return; fi
  git update-ref "refs/heads/$db" "refs/remotes/origin/$db"
  git symbolic-ref HEAD "refs/heads/$db"
  git reset -q --mixed
  # restore only tracked files that are absent from the working tree
  local missing
  missing=$(git ls-files --deleted | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
  git ls-files -z --deleted | xargs -0 -r git checkout -q -- 2>/dev/null
  git branch -q --set-upstream-to="origin/$db" "$db" 2>/dev/null
  local dirty
  dirty=$(git status --porcelain | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
  echo "OK    $dir (branch $db, restored $missing tracked files, $dirty paths dirty/untracked)"
}

# CREDENTIALS.md — key inventory for machine restore

**This file contains NO secret values and must never contain any.** It records *which*
keys each project needs and *where to reissue them*, so a restored machine can be made
functional without guesswork. Values live in your password manager and in the issuing
service's console — nowhere else, by design.

Generated 2026-08-03 by reading key names from `.env` / `.env.example` files. Tracked in
`dotclaude`; mirrored to the SSD.

> **Why this exists.** Every backup correctly excludes credentials. The consequence, found
> during the 2026-08-03 migration audit, is that a perfect restore produces code that
> cannot run and no record of what is missing. This is that record.

## Restore order

Do these in the order you need them, not all at once. Items 1–3 unblock the daily cadence;
the rest can wait until you next touch that project.

| # | Project | File to create | Keys | Reissue from |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `morning-briefing` | `secrets/gmail_credentials.json` | OAuth client JSON (download whole file) | Google Cloud Console → APIs & Services → Credentials → OAuth 2.0 Client IDs |
| 2 | `morning-briefing` | `secrets/gmail_token.json` | generated, not copied | Run the reauth script; it writes this file. **Do not restore from backup** — tokens expire |
| 3 | `DataBase_GPS_Reporting/gps_report` | `.env` | `CATAPULT_TOKEN` | Catapult OpenField → account settings → API token |
| 4 | `ForcePlate_DecisionSystem` | `.env` | `VALD_CLIENT_ID`, `VALD_CLIENT_SECRET`, `VALD_REGION_URL`, `VALD_TEAM_ID` | VALD Hub → API access. Region URL is tenant-specific — copy exactly |
| 5 | `Football/PFF_Data_Project` | `.env` | `PFF_BASE_URL`, `PFF_API_KEY`, `BAYLOR_TEAM_ID` | PFF Ultimate account rep. **Institutional — tied to Baylor's contract** |
| 6 | `PlayerProfiles_FB_03-28-2026` | `.env` | `PERCH_API_TOKEN` | Perch dashboard → integrations |
| 7 | `reMarkale_extract` | `.env` | `GOOGLE_VISION_API_KEY`, `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` | Google Cloud Console → Vision API |
| 8 | `Football/FaceComps/simulator` | `.env.local` | `DATABASE_URL`, `SITE_PASSWORD`, `COOKIE_SECRET`, `CATAPULT_TOKEN` | Supabase → project settings → database. `COOKIE_SECRET` is self-generated (`openssl rand -hex 32`) |
| 9 | `CFB_Victory_Model` | `.env` | `CFBD_API_KEY` | collegefootballdata.com → free API key |
| 10 | `KeystoneOS/zotero-photo-capture` | `.env` | `ZOTERO_API_KEY`, `ZOTERO_USER_ID`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `CROSSREF_MAILTO` | Zotero → Settings → Feeds/API. `CROSSREF_MAILTO` is just your email |

## OAuth connectors — no files, re-auth in the app

These re-authenticate through a browser prompt on first use. Nothing to restore, but
expect to sign in to each once:

Fireflies · Google Drive · Gmail · Google Calendar · Microsoft 365 (Baylor) · Supabase ·
Vercel · Zotero · reMarkable · Anthropic (Claude Code) · OpenAI (Codex) · GitHub (`gh auth login`)

## Which of these survive leaving Baylor

| Survives | Does not |
|---|---|
| CFBD, Zotero, Anthropic, OpenAI, GitHub, Google (personal), reMarkable, Supabase, Vercel | PFF (Baylor contract), Catapult (Baylor tenant), VALD (Baylor tenant), Perch (Baylor tenant), Microsoft 365 |

Institutional keys stop working when the contract or your account does. That is expected
and correct — do not attempt to preserve them. The *code* that uses them is yours; the
*access* is Baylor's.

## Known live issue

**2026-08-03 — Outlook auth for `morning-briefing` is expired.** The 08:19 brief sent with
0 email threads. Reauthenticate rather than carrying this into the migration:

```powershell
& "$env:USERPROFILE\Desktop\DEV\morning-briefing\scripts\reauth.bat"
```

On macOS this script needs porting to `.sh` — see `MIGRATION-MACOS.md` Step 8.

## Accepted exception — FaceComps `.env.local` on the SSD

**Decided by Eric, 2026-08-04, with the exposure stated.** `D:\AssistantBackup\DEV-nonrepo\Football\FaceComps\simulator\.env.local`
remains on the external drive, holding live values for `DATABASE_URL`, `SITE_PASSWORD`,
`COOKIE_SECRET`, and `CATAPULT_TOKEN`.

This is the one deliberate departure from "no credentials in any backup." The reasoning
was that the old machine — the only other copy — is being decommissioned during the
2026-08-04 migration, so purging risked losing the values outright.

Consequences, recorded so they are not rediscovered by surprise:

- The drive is unencrypted NTFS. Anyone who plugs it in can read these four values.
- If the drive is lost, checked as luggage, or left unattended, rotate all four:
  Supabase (`DATABASE_URL`), the site password, and the Catapult token. `COOKIE_SECRET`
  needs no service — regenerate with `openssl rand -hex 32`.
- Once these values are in the password manager, delete the SSD copy and remove this
  section. The backup script's deny-list already prevents it being re-copied, so deleting
  it is permanent and safe.

Every other credential found on the drive was purged on 2026-08-04: `morning-briefing/secrets/owa-profile`
(7,633 files — a live authenticated Outlook browser profile with Cookies and Login Data)
and an `edge-profile` under `SpecialRequests` (272 files). Both were session state that
re-authentication regenerates.

## Rules

1. **Never** commit a value to this file or any repo. `.env` files stay gitignored.
2. When you add a project that needs a key, add a row here in the same session.
3. `gmail_token.json` and any other *generated* token is regenerated, never restored — a
   restored token is usually already expired and fails confusingly.
4. If a key leaks, rotate it at the issuing service first, then update your password
   manager. This file needs no change; it names keys, not values.

"""Run once: opens a real Chromium window so you can sign in to Outlook Web.
Saved session sits at the profile path configured in config.toml.
Check 'stay signed in' / 'trust this device' when prompted."""
import asyncio
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from playwright.async_api import async_playwright


async def main(profile_dir: Path):
    profile_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    async with async_playwright() as p:
        ctx = await p.chromium.launch_persistent_context(
            user_data_dir=str(profile_dir), headless=False
        )

"""Run once: opens a real Chromium window so you can sign in to Outlook Web.
Saved session sits at the profile path configured in config.toml.
Check 'stay signed in' / 'trust this device' when prompted."""
import asyncio
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from playwright.async_api import async_playwright


async def main(profile_dir: Path):
    profile_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    async with async_playwright() as p:
        ctx = await p.chromium.launch_persistent_context(
            user_data_dir=str(profile_dir), headless=False
        )
        page = await ctx.new_page()
        await page.goto("https://outlook.office.com/mail/")
        print("Sign in, then close the window when the inbox is visible.")
        await page.wait_for_event("close", timeout=0)
        await ctx.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    profile = Path(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else Path("./secrets/owa-profile")
    asyncio.run(main(profile))

exit=1
---script head---
# Runs the KeystoneOS morning packet + dashboard refresh. Called by the
# 'KeystoneOS Morning' scheduled task; safe to run manually.
$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
$keystone = Join-Path $PSScriptRoot "keystone.ps1"
$log = Join-Path $PSScriptRoot "../outputs/morning/cadence.log"
try {
    & $keystone morning *>> $log
    & $keystone meeting-sync *>> $log
    # Portfolio dashboard daily re-render (project-triage/render.py). Runs
    # before snapshot so the snapshot's Front Burner section reflects today's
    # pulse, not yesterday's. Non-fatal: a render failure here must never
    # break the rest of the morning cadence.
    try {
        & "C:\Users\eric_rash\AppData\Local\Python\bin\python.exe" "C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\project-triage\render.py" 2>&1 |
            ForEach-Object { Add-Content $log "[portfolio] $_" }
    } catch {
        Add-Content $log "[portfolio] render failed: $_"
    }
    & $keystone snapshot *>> $log
    & $keystone dashboard *>> $log
    & $keystone cockpit *>> $log
    # Drift guard: cadence keeps the generated layer fresh, but nothing was
    # watching the hand-written layer go stale. Never fails the cadence.
    & (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot "os-freshness.ps1") *>> $log
    # Ritual guard: a skipped ritual leaves no error, only an absence. Both
    # rituals froze for 49 days before anything noticed.
    & (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot "ritual-check.ps1") *>> $log
    Add-Content $log "[$(Get-Date -Format o)] cadence OK"
} catch {
    Add-Content $log "[$(Get-Date -Format o)] cadence FAILED: $_"
    exit 1
}

    & $keystone morning *>> $log
    & $keystone meeting-sync *>> $log
    # Portfolio dashboard daily re-render (project-triage/render.py). Runs

    # pulse, not yesterday's. Non-fatal: a render failure here must never
    # break the rest of the morning cadence.
    try {
        & "C:\Users\eric_rash\AppData\Local\Python\bin\python.exe" "C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\project-triage\render.py" 2>&1 |
            ForEach-Object { Add-Content $log "[portfolio] $_" }
    } catch {
        Add-Content $log "[portfolio] render failed: $_"
    }
    & $keystone snapshot *>> $log
    & $keystone dashboard *>> $log
    & $keystone cockpit *>> $log
    # Drift guard: cadence keeps the generated layer fresh, but nothing was
    # watching the hand-written layer go stale. Never fails the cadence.
    & (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot "os-freshness.ps1") *>> $log
    # Ritual guard: a skipped ritual leaves no error, only an absence. Both
    # rituals froze for 49 days before anything noticed.
    & (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot "ritual-check.ps1") *>> $log
    Add-Content $log "[$(Get-Date -Format o)] cadence OK"
} catch {
    Add-Content $log "[$(Get-Date -Format o)] cadence FAILED: $_"
    exit 1
}

- **Prefer the PowerShell tool over Bash** for shell operations on this machine. Bash frequently fails silently (exit 1, empty output) in this Windows setup — if a Bash call returns empty/nonzero with no clear error, switch to PowerShell immediately instead of retrying.
- Don't rely on PATH inside Bash for these binaries — use the verified full paths:

  - uv: `C:\Users\eric_rash\.local\bin\uv.exe`

  - Node: `C:\Program Files\nodejs\node.exe`

# Workflow Expectations

- When asked to **create, merge, or consolidate an artifact** (calendar, deck, doc), the expected deliverable is always a produced file. Verify what exists first, then create the artifact regardless — never conclude with "it already exists" instead of delivering the file.

# graphify
- **graphify** (`~/.claude/skills/graphify/SKILL.md`) - any input to knowledge graph. Trigger: `/graphify`
When the user types `/graphify`, invoke the Skill tool with `skill: "graphify"` before doing anything else.

# Memory System

This is a two-tier memory system. **Read this before doing any memory reads or writes.**

## Tier A — Per-project structured facts (existing)
Lives at `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`. One file per durable fact, indexed by `MEMORY.md`. The harness auto-injects this. Continue to **write** here for stable facts: user profile entries, project-specific conventions, feedback rules. This tier is indexed by memsearch (Tier B) so it's also recallable cross-project.

## Tier B — Global working memory (new)
Lives at `~/.claude/global-memory/`. Loaded at every session start regardless of cwd:
- `USER.md` (~1.4 KB cap) — durable user profile
- `MEMORY.md` (~2.5 KB cap) — active threads, environment notes, pending decisions
- `transcripts/YYYY-MM-DD.md` — auto-captured turn summaries (Stop hook)

## Daily compiled logs (separate system)
Daily decision/lesson/action summaries are produced by `claude-memory-compiler` (its own SessionEnd/PreCompact hooks) and live at `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/{YYYY-MM-DD}.md`. These are injected by the compiler's own SessionStart hook — do **not** write to them manually, and do **not** read them eagerly; treat the injected snapshot as the source of truth.

## Session Startup (silent — do not output anything)

On every session start, read these files silently, in this order:
1. `~/.claude/global-memory/USER.md`
2. `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md`
3. `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — if non-empty, surface the contents to the user once on the first response of the session, then continue normally. This file should normally be empty; entries indicate hook failures (e.g. memsearch flush patch was stripped after a pip upgrade).

These are a **frozen snapshot** — loaded once. Mid-session writes persist to disk but take effect next session. This preserves the prefix cache. Total injected at startup is small (~3,000 tokens); never load more than this proactively.

## Memory Budget

- `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md`: **2,500 character cap**. Before writing, check `wc -c`. If over cap, consolidate existing entries before adding.
- `~/.claude/global-memory/USER.md`: **1,375 character cap**. Same rule.
- Mid-session writes appear in context **next session**, not this one.

## Memory Write — which tier to use

Decide tier first, then write.

**Tier A (per-project structured)** — when the fact is:
- A durable claim about the user (role, preferences, working style) → update or add a `user_*.md` file
- A stable project convention or gotcha (e.g. "Catapult API v6 uses /stats not v4 /statistics") → `project_*.md`
- A feedback rule that should govern future behavior → `feedback_*.md`

Write the file with proper frontmatter (`name`, `description`, `metadata.type`) and add a one-line pointer to `~/.claude/projects/C--Users-eric-rash/memory/MEMORY.md`.

**Tier B (global scratchpad)** — when the fact is:
- An active thread (currently-in-progress work that will be referenced soon)
- An environment note (URLs, tool versions, project structure currently in play)
- A pending decision

When the user says "remember this", "note that", "update memory", "save this", "forget about":
1. Decide tier (durable+structured = A; active+scratchpad = B)
2. Read the target file in full
3. Dedup check (substring scan)
4. Cap check (`wc -c`) for Tier B
5. If over cap: consolidate (merge similar entries, prune stale) before adding
6. Write
7. Confirm: "Saved — will be active from next session."

For **remove**: confirm with the user before deleting.

## Memory Retrieval — tiered ladder

When the user asks about past context, decisions, or "did we already…?":

1. **Tier 0** — scan what's already in context (USER.md, MEMORY.md, today's log). Zero cost.
2. **L1** — `memsearch search "query" --top-k 5`. Hybrid vector + keyword. Finds semantic matches across all indexed paths (Tier A files, daily logs, transcripts).
3. **L2** — `memsearch expand <chunk_hash>`. Full markdown section around a hit.
4. **L3** — `memsearch transcript <session_id>`. Raw dialogue, last resort.
5. **Fallback** — "I don't have a record of that."

Only escalate if the previous tier didn't answer the question. Don't run memsearch when the answer is already in the injected snapshot.

## Tier boundary — when in doubt

Ask: "Will this fact still be true and useful in 3 months, across multiple projects?"
- **Yes** → Tier A
- **No / only matters right now** → Tier B

attachment.content:
- advisor: Consult a grounded domain advisor built from your curated book library. Answers ONLY from ingested library entries, cites every claim, and explicitly separates grounded knowledge from general knowledge. Use when the user says "ask my <domain> advisor", "/advisor <domain> <question>", "what would my library say about…", or consults a standing advisor. Domains live in SecondBrain/Knowledge/library/advisors/.
- articulation-skill: Help users articulate complex ideas clearly and simply to non-technical audiences using proven communication frameworks. Use when users need to explain technical concepts, structure presentations or writing, create clear documentation, improve communication clarity, or translate jargon into accessible language. Triggers include requests like "help me explain this clearly", "how do I structure this presentation", "make this less technical", "help me articulate this idea", or any request to simplify complex communication.
- backtrack: Use when the agent just missed something that was there — said "I don't have access to that" or "I couldn't find it" about a file, note, or fact you know exists, or searched for a long time before finding something it should have hit immediately. Also use on "backtrack", "why didn't you find that", "you should have found that", "trace your search". Makes the agent reconstruct its own search path, find the real cause of the miss, and fix the routing so the same miss cannot recur.
- capture-insight: Capture a story, win, or lesson the user just shared as a permanent atomic note in the SecondBrain vault. Use when the user tells a story or lesson and says "capture this", "save this win/lesson", "that's worth a note", or "/capture-insight". For end-of-day structured capture use interview-me; for whole-project distillation use harvest; for plain facts use memory-write.
- caveman: Ultra-compressed communication mode. Cuts token usage ~75% by dropping filler, articles, and pleasantries while keeping full technical accuracy. Use when user says "caveman mode", "talk like caveman", "use caveman", "less tokens", "be brief", or invokes /caveman.
- claude-stack-doctor: Health-check Eric's automation/memory stack in one pass — scheduled tasks (KeystoneOS Morning, AgySync, MorningBriefing), Python venvs, memsearch, memory-compiler flush pipeline, and hook error log — and diagnose what's silently broken. Use when the user says "/claude-stack-doctor", "stack doctor", "is my stack healthy", "did my scheduled tasks run", "check the memory pipeline", "why didn't the briefing run", or when closeout/morning sessions should verify automation health.
- closeout: End-of-session sign-off ritual. Sweeps loose ends, commits and pushes what needs it, verifies memory capture, writes a cross-harness handoff, and reports "clear to sign off" or what's still open. Use when the user says "/closeout", "any loose ends?", "am I good to sign off?", "close out for the night", "closing out", "goodnight", "wrap up for the day", or asks for a system health check before leaving.
- decision-toolkit: Generate structured decision-making tools — step-by-step guides, bias checkers, scenario explorers, and interactive dashboards. Use when facing significant choices requiring systematic analysis. Supports multiple cognitive styles and output formats.
- design-academy-skill: Apply data storytelling and dashboard design principles to any visualization, dashboard, report, or data-driven presentation. Use when building or critiquing a dashboard, designing a report layout, preparing a data-driven deck, or when the user mentions "dashboard design", "data storytelling", "making data clear", "audience-first design", "KPI layout" — including when they are clearly showing data to an audience without asking for design help.
- diagram-generator: Generate professional color-coded Excalidraw diagrams (.excalidraw JSON files, editable at excalidraw.com) from plain-English descriptions. Use when the user asks for a flowchart, architecture diagram, process or flow diagram, mind map, timeline, or before/after comparison diagram, or says "diagram this", "draw the architecture", "map out this process". NOT for styled interactive HTML explainer pages — use visual-explainer for those.
- everything-search: Instant filename search across all Windows drives via the Everything CLI (indexed, near-zero latency, full Everything search syntax). Use when the user asks to find a file or folder by name anywhere on disk ("where is X", "find all *.pptx modified last month", "locate the folder called Y"), or when Glob over a huge or unknown directory tree would be slow. Filename and metadata search only — for searching file contents use Grep.
- fable-mode: Use PROACTIVELY when a task has many layers — dependent steps, unknowns that could change the approach, debugging where the first theory may be wrong, or anything needing verification before handoff. Also when a task keeps failing or stalling, or on "fable mode", "think like Fable", "use the Fable method", "work like Fable", "slow down and do this right", "think this through first". Loads Fable 5's five-gate task loop and standing habits.
- fact-checker: Systematic fact verification and misinformation identification using evidence-based analysis.
Use when: verifying claims, checking facts, identifying misinformation, evaluating source credibility,
or when user asks to "fact check", "verify", "is this true", or mentions claims that need validation.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- firecrawl: Search, scrape, and interact with the web via the Firecrawl CLI. Use whenever the user wants to search the web, research a topic, scrape a webpage, grab content from a URL, crawl documentation, download a site, or interact with pages needing clicks or logins — including "fetch this page", "pull the content from", "get the page at https://". Real-time search with full page content. NOT for local files, git, deployments, or code editing.
- firecrawl-build-onboarding: Get Firecrawl credentials and SDK setup into a project. Use when an application needs `FIRECRAWL_API_KEY`, when an agent should add Firecrawl to `.env`, when the user wants to authenticate Firecrawl for app code, or when choosing the first SDK and docs for a new Firecrawl integration. This skill includes its own browser auth flow, so it does not depend on the website onboarding skill.
- fireflies-intake: One-command Fireflies pipeline — sync new meeting transcripts into the SecondBrain vault, rename generically-titled meetings, then report exactly what was ingested. Use when the user says "/fireflies-intake", "ingest my recent fireflies meetings", "sync meetings that aren't in the second brain yet", "pull in the new meetings", "meeting ingestion", or asks whether all recent meetings have been ingested.
- five-slides-generator: Generate a complete '5 Slides in 5 Minutes' PowerPoint deck on any topic for Baylor Athletics Applied Performance. Use this skill whenever the user mentions '5 slides,' '5 slides in 5 minutes,' or gives a topic they want a Performance School deck on. Also trigger when they ask for a cross-functional staff presentation, a quick sport science deck, or any short educational deck in the established series format (CMJ, GPS, VBT are prior examples). This skill handles everything: web research, 5-slide narrative structure, pptxgenjs code generation, .pptx file build, and QA.
- forecast-capture: Capture and freeze the CFB Victory Model's pre-game forecasts before kickoff, then report what moved since last week. Run every Wednesday during the season. Use when the user says "/forecast-capture", "capture the forecast", "freeze this week's predictions", "run the CFB capture", "did we capture this week", or asks whether the weekly model snapshot has been taken.
- frontend-slides: Create stunning, animation-rich HTML presentations from scratch or by converting PowerPoint files. Use when the user says "make a presentation", "create slides", "slide deck", "build a deck about", "I need to present", wants to convert a PPT/PPTX to web, or needs slides for a talk/pitch. Helps non-designers discover their aesthetic through visual exploration rather than abstract choices. (For the Baylor "5 Slides in 5 Minutes" PPTX series, use five-slides-generator; for HTML concept explainers, use visual-explainer.)
- game-film-timestamps: Fix wrong startTime/endTime values in football game film JSON exported from Hudl, DVSport, or similar. Fetches correct wall-clock timestamps from the ESPN API and writes corrected copies. Use whenever the user mentions fixing or correcting play-by-play timestamps in game film JSON, or has files with "OFF", "DEF", or "KICKS" in the filename and mentions timestamps or time issues.
- graphify: Turn any input — code, docs, papers, images, or a whole folder — into a navigable knowledge graph with clustered communities, interactive HTML, GraphRAG-ready JSON, and an audit report. Use when the user types /graphify, says "graphify this", "build a knowledge graph of X", "map this codebase/docs as a graph", or wants to query, extend, or explain an existing graph (/graphify query, path, explain, add, --update, --watch).
- Harvest: Distill a finished project into evergreen Knowledge/ articles in the SecondBrain vault and log the shipped artifact in the output ledger. Use when the user says "/harvest <project>", "harvest this project", "distill what we learned from X", declares a project finished/shipped/done, or when a session ends with a clearly shipped deliverable worth recording.
- html-to-pdf: Render any local HTML report, deck, or dashboard to a print-ready PDF via headless Chrome — replaces the manual Ctrl+P → Save as PDF ritual. Use when the user says "export this to PDF", "print version", "PDF for the coaches", "make this printable", or a coach-facing HTML deliverable needs a shareable/printable copy.
- humanizer: Remove signs of AI-generated writing from text. Use when editing or reviewing
text to make it sound more natural and human-written. Based on Wikipedia's
comprehensive "Signs of AI writing" guide. Detects and fixes patterns including:
inflated symbolism, promotional language, superficial -ing analyses, vague
attributions, em dash overuse, rule of three, AI vocabulary words, negative
parallelisms, and excessive conjunctive phrases.
- impeccable: Use when the user wants to design, redesign, shape, critique, audit, polish, clarify, distill, harden, optimize, adapt, animate, colorize, extract, or otherwise improve a frontend interface. Covers websites, landing pages, dashboards, product UI, app shells, components, forms, settings, onboarding, and empty states. Handles UX review, visual hierarchy, information architecture, cognitive load, accessibility, performance, responsive behavior, theming, anti-patterns, typography, fonts, spacing, layout, alignment, color, motion, micro-interactions, UX copy, error states, edge cases, i18n, and reusable design systems or tokens. Also use for bland designs that need to become bolder or more delightful, loud designs that should become quieter, live browser iteration on UI elements, or ambitious visual effects that should feel technically extraordinary. Not for backend-only or non-UI tasks.
- improve-system: Audit the SecondBrain vault for rot — stale seed notes, conflicting claims, and duplicate notes — and propose merge/archive/update actions. Use when the user says "/improve-system", "audit my notes", "audit the vault", "find stale/duplicate notes", or "clean up my second brain". For mining sessions for missed learnings use session-miner; for capturing a win/lesson use capture-insight; for improving a skill use write-a-skill.
- ingest-book: Ingest a book (PDF/EPUB full-text, Kindle highlights, or framework-only from a physical book) into the SecondBrain library as atomized, citable advisor entries. Use when the user wants to "ingest a book", "add a book to my library/advisors", "/ingest-book", or points at a book file for the advisor system. For articles/transcripts/general resources use ingest-resource instead.
- ingest-resource: Ingest any article, YouTube link, transcript, PDF, or note into the SecondBrain vault — routes it to Knowledge/ (stable info) or Projects/ (active work), adds a summary block, and cross-links related notes with [[wikilinks]]. Use when the user shares a URL, file, or pasted content and says "ingest", "save this", "add to my vault/second brain", "/ingest-resource", or drops a resource with intent to keep it.
- interview-me: End-of-workday structured interview that distills the user's day into atomic permanent notes for their SecondBrain Obsidian vault. NOT a journaling app — produces curated synthesis notes, not stream-of-consciousness. Use when the user types `/interview-me`, says "interview me", "let's debrief", "end of day interview", "process my day", "wrap up today", or otherwise asks to capture their workday for their second brain.
- library-review: Review a book-library domain for gaps, contested entries, and missing coverage, and propose new entries. Manual loop — proposes, you approve. Use when the user says "review my library", "/library-review <domain>", "what's missing from my <domain> advisor", or after a batch of ingestion.
- loop-designer: Designs safe agentic loops from recurring workflows, producing a Loop Card with discovery inputs, durable state, generator task, evaluator checks, human checkpoint, permissions, caps, and schedule. Use when the user says "make this a loop", "turn this workflow into a loop", "design a loop", "loopify this", or asks whether a repeated workflow should become an automation/skill/cadence.
- meeting-prep: Pre-meeting readiness brief for a project. Verifies the latest decisions actually landed in the artifacts, lists what changed since the last meeting, flags open questions, and points to every deliverable path. Use when the user says "/meeting-prep <project>", "I have a meeting with <person> — are we in a good spot on <project>?", "verify we're up to speed before the meeting", "get me ready for this afternoon's meeting", or names an upcoming coach/staff meeting and asks for project status.
- meeting-sync: Pulls new Fireflies meeting transcripts into the SecondBrain vault as structured markdown summaries, and audits vault filenames for drift against current Fireflies titles. Idempotent — re-running won't duplicate. Use when the user says "sync meetings", "pull latest meetings", "/meeting-sync", "update meeting notes", "any new meetings?", or when invoked by the weekly-review skill. Also use for filename drift questions — "are any meeting files misnamed?", "did a meeting get renamed after export?", "why is this meeting titled differently in Fireflies than in the vault?", "audit the meeting filenames".
- memory-write: Saves durable facts to the two-tier memory system at ~/.claude/global-memory/ and ~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/. Triggers on "remember this", "note that", "update memory", "save this", "forget about". Picks the correct tier (structured per-project vs global scratchpad), then handles add / replace / remove with dedup and character-cap enforcement.
- name-meetings: Detects Fireflies meetings with generic titles (empty, "Zoom Meeting", "Recording", date-only, etc.), proposes structured names based on AI summary + participants, and applies approved renames via the Fireflies API. Use when user says "/name-meetings", "name my meetings", "rename untitled meetings", "fix meeting titles", "my meetings have no names", or when invoked by meeting-sync.
- pbir-report-builder: Generates Power BI report pages, visuals, and IBCS-compliant variance charts by writing PBIR JSON into PBIP project folders. Use whenever the user wants to create a Power BI page, add visuals, generate KPI cards, build charts, tables or dashboard layouts, or mentions 'PBIR', 'IBCS', 'variance chart', 'variance table', 'actual vs plan'.
- pp-catapult-openfield-connect: Every Catapult GPS metric — ACWR, velocity benchmarks, load reports — from one command via catapult-openfield-connect-pp-cli, with a local SQLite database for offline analysis. Trigger phrases: `check ACWR for the squad`, `what is the player load from today session`, `compare last two matches`, `who is at injury risk`, `generate a weekly load report`, `sync Catapult data`, `use catapult-openfield-connect-pp-cli`, `run catapult CLI`.
- pp-espn: ESPN sports CLI — live scores, standings, team stats, schedules, polls, rankings, and game summaries (box score, leaders, scoring plays, odds, win probability) across NFL / NBA / MLB / NHL / NCAA / MLS / EPL / WNBA. Use for 'what's the score of the Lakers game', 'Patriots schedule this week', 'NFL standings', 'box score', head-to-head comparisons, 'who's on top of the AP poll'. No API key required.

Trigger phrases: `what should I watch tonight`, `where can I stream <title>`, `rate <title>`, `compare <title> and <title>`, `what's <person>'s filmography`, `plan a <franchise> marathon`, `use movie-goat`, `run movie-goat`.

Trigger phrases: `find me a recipe for <dish>`, `best <dish> recipe`, `what can I make with these ingredients`, `nutrition facts for <ingredient>`, `use recipe-goat`, `run recipe-goat`. Read-only: search, compare, export — never ordering or purchasing.

Trigger phrases: `sync my Zotero library`, `check Zotero auth`, `pull updates from Zotero`, `set my Zotero API key`, `run Zotero doctor`, `use zotero-research-library`, `run zotero cli`.

Use to plan a complex task, design a process, scope a project, or stress-test a plan, and on "I want to build", "let's plan", "help me think through", "I have an idea for", "scope this out", "interview me about this", "I need a skill that". Deliverable is the spec; hand skill specs to write-a-skill.

Triggers on "/project", "new idea:", "log progress on", "project update", "add to my project inbox", "show my projects", "re-rank my projects", "set the stage on", "mark <project> as spec'd/planned/shipped".
- project-triage: Generate the DEV/ project triage HTML dashboard for today (or backfill a missed day). Scans top-level folders in ~/Desktop/DEV, classifies each by activity heuristics, applies the user's curated purpose/action prose where present, and surfaces drift between curated and current state. Use when the user says "project triage", "/project-triage", "run my project review", "dev dashboard", "what's open in DEV", "morning review", or asks to see the open-projects HTML.
- research-assistant: Deep-dive an external topic and produce a structured, sourced research document saved to disk. Use when the user says "deep dive", "look into", "investigate", "what do we know about", "give me a report on", or "I need to understand" about a topic outside the current codebase. Produces a saved markdown file, not a chat response. NOT for questions answerable from the local codebase or memory, and NOT for multi-perspective briefings (use storm-research) or formal cited analytical reports (use firecrawl-deep-research).
- roast: Use when someone asks to roast an idea, pressure-test or stress-test an idea, validate a business idea, "convene the council", get a brutal second opinion before building something, or says "/roast". Spins up a 5-persona council that attacks the idea from every angle, then a Judge returns one GO / RESHAPE / KILL verdict with the cheapest test to de-risk it.

Produces a chat-only handoff covering decisions, shipped changes, key files, running state, verification steps, deferrals, and open questions so a fresh agent can continue seamlessly.
- session-miner: Mine recent Claude Code sessions for learnings that never got captured — repeated corrections, decisions with rationale, gotchas, and workflows worth turning into skills — and route each to memory, the vault, or a skill edit. Use when the user says "/session-miner", "what did we miss", "review recent sessions", "mine my history", or "anything from this week worth keeping?".

Use when reviewing a skill before installation or publication, auditing a skill that produces or verifies outputs, checking whether a skill's declared resources exist, or assigning an objective PASS, FAIL, DEGRADED, or 0-10 grade.
- sports-science-research-grounding: Use automatically for substantive questions about sport science, return to play or sport, rehabilitation, strength and conditioning, workload, recovery, testing, athlete health, injury, performance, research-backed answers, and Zotero full-library batch processing. Searches the user's Zotero library first, clearly labels external peer-reviewed fallback sources, and applies tier-aware model routing during bounded batch work.
- starter-design-tokens: Build a design tokens file with your brand colors, fonts, and visual style. Triggers on: "design tokens", "brand colors", "brand fonts", "visual identity", "set up my brand look", "how things look". Produces brand_context/design-tokens.md.
- starter-icp-positioning: Build your ICP and positioning in one pass — who it's for, what you stand for, and what you're against. Triggers on: "ICP", "ideal customer", "positioning", "who is my customer", "target audience", "what do I stand for". Produces brand_context/icp.md.
- starter-voice-profile: Build a voice profile from real writing examples so Claude writes like you. Best for topics where multiple viewpoints and fact-checked claims matter; overkill for a simple factual lookup.

- to-prd: Turn the current conversation into a PRD and publish it to the project issue tracker. Use only when the user explicitly asks to create, synthesize, or publish a PRD from context already discussed; do not trigger for ordinary planning or implementation.

- web-scraping: Semantic web search with Exa, plus scripted Firecrawl scraping, using local Python scripts and .env API keys. Use when the user says "/web-scraping", asks for semantic/neural search ("find pages similar to X", "research papers about Y semantically"), or wants the scripted discover-then-extract pipeline (exa_search.py → firecrawl_scrape.py) with output saved to files. Use when user says "/weekly-review", "weekly review", "Friday review", "let's do this week's review", "weekly synthesis", or "what should I work on next week?".

# Weekly unattended stack-doctor run (Task Scheduler: KeystoneOS-StackDoctor).
# Runs the read-only stack-check and, ONLY on failure, appends a one-line
# summary to global-memory .errors.log — which every Claude session surfaces
# at startup per CLAUDE.md. Silence in that file means the check passed.
# Full output of the most recent run is always kept in last-weekly-run.log.

$check = Join-Path $PSScriptRoot 'stack-check.ps1'
$out = & 'C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe' -NoProfile -File $check 2>&1 | Out-String
$failed = $LASTEXITCODE -ne 0

Set-Content -Path (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot 'last-weekly-run.log') -Value $out -Encoding utf8

if ($failed) {
    $verdict = (($out -split "`r?`n") | Where-Object { $_ -match '^\d+ issue' } | Select-Object -First 1)
    if (-not $verdict) { $verdict = 'check failed (no VERDICT line — see last-weekly-run.log)' }
    $stamp = Get-Date -Format o
    $entry = "[$stamp] stack-doctor weekly: $verdict — details in ~\.claude\skills\claude-stack-doctor\scripts\last-weekly-run.log; run /claude-stack-doctor to fix"
    Add-Content -Path "$env:USERPROFILE\.claude\global-memory\transcripts\.errors.log" -Value $entry -Encoding utf8
}
exit 0

cat > ~/.claude/skills/everything-search/SKILL.md <<'EOF'
---
name: everything-search
description: Instant filename search across the whole Mac via mdfind (Spotlight index, near-zero latency). Use when the user asks to find a file or folder by name anywhere on disk ("where is X", "find all *.pptx modified last month", "locate the folder called Y"), or when Glob over a huge or unknown directory tree would be slow. Filename and metadata search only — for searching file contents use Grep.
---

# Everything Search (macOS: mdfind)

Query the Spotlight index via `mdfind`. Spotlight indexes filenames and metadata
on all local volumes in real time, so searches return in milliseconds where
Glob/find would crawl for minutes. (This skill was originally built on the
Windows Everything CLI; `mdfind` is the macOS equivalent.)

## Common queries

```bash
# Filename contains a word (fastest, most common)
mdfind -name "forceplate"

# Exact-ish filename with extension
mdfind -name "cadence.log"

# Limit to a directory tree
mdfind -onlyin ~/DEV -name "requirements"

# All files of a type modified in the last 30 days
mdfind 'kMDItemFSName == "*.pptx" && kMDItemFSContentChangeDate >= $time.today(-30)'

# Folders only, by name
mdfind 'kMDItemContentType == "public.folder" && kMDItemFSName == "*Victory*"'

# Count instead of listing
mdfind -count -name "SKILL.md"
```

## Notes and pitfalls

- **External drives**: exFAT/USB volumes are often NOT indexed. Check with
  `mdutil -s /Volumes/<name>`; enable with `sudo mdutil -i on /Volumes/<name>`,
  or fall back to `find /Volumes/<name> -iname '*pattern*'`.
- **Hidden/system paths** (`~/Library`, dotfiles) are largely excluded from
  Spotlight. Fall back to `find` or Glob for those.
- Metadata attribute names: `mdls <file>` shows every attribute a file carries;
  use those keys in query syntax.
- Results stream full absolute paths — pipe through `head` for broad terms.

## When NOT to use

- Content search inside files → Grep.
- Small known directory → Glob is fine.
- Freshly created files may lag the index by a few seconds.
EOF

**CHECKPOINT 8** — Phase 7 is now fully complete and Phase 8 is done. Here's the report.

## launchd agents: all 8 loaded, exit status 0

`morning` (daily 06:00), `reconcile` (daily 07:00 + login), `agysync` (6-hourly), `rituals` (weekdays 17:00 + Fri 15:30), `adjudicate` (Sun 02:30), `morningbriefing` (daily 07:20), `stackdoctor` (Mon 10:30), and `dailybackup` (daily 00:30) — the last one loaded only after the ported backup script proved itself. MsysKeepAlive retired as planned.

## The big Phase 8 discovery: the real skills were never restored

The runbook assumed `erash11/claude-skills` on GitHub carried your skills — but `~/.claude/skills` on this Mac held a *different, pre-existing* 72-skill set (dotclaude gitignores `skills/` as a nested repo, so Phase 2's clone silently never happened). The old machine's **real 65-skill set — including claude-stack-doctor, closeout, project-triage, graphify, and all the pp-\* skills — existed only on the drive** at `claude/skills` (a git repo with 43 uncommitted edits). I restored it additively; `~/.claude/skills` is now the claude-skills repo with 135 skill dirs (both sets; only `tdd` collided — drive version won). The drive's `claude/agents`, `config`, `scripts`, `hooks` were also restored additively — Phase 3 had skipped all of them.

## Ported / fixed

- **daily-backup.ps1**: full macOS port (original kept as `.win-orig`) — robocopy→rsync, **every destination now additive** (no mirror), forward-slash credential deny-list (now provably catching the `.env` files that leaked to the drive), Google Drive + Baylor OneDrive repointed to `~/Library/CloudStorage/...`, SSD target set to a placeholder `/Volumes/CRASHBOX` with `optional:true` per the runbook — it warns, never touches the transport USB stick. A dry run is mid-flight (slow first pass against cloud filesystems) and has already validated repo sync, snapshots, and manifest coverage. It also caught and I resolved a real `global-memory` divergence (union-merged, pushed clean).
- **Windows-isms swept**: ~30 files across KeystoneOS scripts + data JSONs, memory-compiler, settings.json hooks, global CLAUDE.md (PowerShell-first rule dropped), all skill files — zero `C:\`/`USERPROFILE` refs remain. `fix-msys-ad-stall.ps1` deleted.
- **Skill triage**: `everything-search` rewritten on `mdfind`; `claude-stack-doctor` rewritten against `launchctl` (live run works — its findings drove several fixes); `html-to-pdf` pointed at macOS Chrome; `project-triage`/`forecast-capture` depathed, `render.py` fixed and verified.
- **SecondBrain** made a real git repo again (Phase 3 rsync had dropped `.git`); 881 phantom "modified" files were exFAT mode-bit noise, fixed with `core.fileMode false` across all restored repos. Its 218 real newer-than-GitHub changes will auto-commit on the first nightly backup.
- **Go CLIs**: 5 of 7 installed (`espn`, `fireflies`, `flight-goat`, `movie-goat`, `recipe-goat`). `catapult-openfield-connect` and `zotero-research-library` built from a local `~/printing-press` source tree that exists in **no backup** — outstanding.
- **A trap the runbook couldn't know**: OneDrive on this Mac is Files-On-Demand, and KeystoneOS's discovery scan ran `git status` inside it — hydrating gigabytes and hanging the morning cadence for 40+ minutes. I disabled the `baylor_workdrive` discovery root and memory source with recorded reasons; re-enable after pinning that folder "Always Keep on This Device". After the fix, morning-cadence completes cleanly.

## Still outstanding (carried to Phase 9)

- Your two interactive auths: `gmail_auth.py` and `reauth.sh` (both need your browser)
- Milvus/memsearch full config (deferred day-one per runbook; basic search works)
- The two source-less Go CLIs; `gws` CLI for the backup's cloud-side check (optional)
- Skill-tax warning: 133 skills = ~16k tokens of descriptions (205% of the old budget) — a natural consequence of carrying both skill sets; deciding what to archive is yours
- The drive-credential deletion question from Checkpoint 6 (still awaiting your confirmation)

Say the word and I'll run **Phase 9** — the verification checklist plus correcting START-HERE.md/MIGRATION-MACOS.md from everything learned, committing to dotclaude, and copying back to the drive.

from pathlib import Path

SCOPES = ["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.readonly"]

Done. To activate it, type **`/reload-plugins`** (or it loads next session) — it'll appear as `cli-printing-press@skills-dir` with the `/printing-press` command available.

Why it didn't transfer, for the record: it was installed on the old machine as a *plugin* (in the plugin cache, which isn't backed up — correctly, since plugins reinstall from their marketplaces), and the normal reinstall path broke on this Mac because the installer clones over SSH and this machine has no SSH keys yet. The HTTPS clone into the skills directory sidesteps that entirely, and since it's a real git clone, it updates with a simple `git pull`.

Bonus: this also reopens the path to the two missing CLIs — `catapult-openfield-connect-pp-cli` and `zotero-research-library-pp-cli` were *generated* by this very tool into `~/printing-press` on the old machine. Once the plugin is loaded, `/printing-press` can regenerate them from their API specs whenever you want them back.

# /printing-press-reprint

Regenerate an existing printed CLI under the current machine. The user gives
a CLI name and (optionally) reasons for the reprint. This skill ensures the
prior CLI is locally present, recommends whether to reuse or redo prior
research, and hands off to `/printing-press` with the context the
novel-features subagent needs to reconcile prior features against the
current machine — keep, reframe, or drop with reasons, never silent.

```bash
/printing-press-reprint notion
/printing-press-reprint cal.com  the new MCP intent surface landed and the prior CLI ships endpoint-mirror only
/printing-press-reprint allrecipes
```

## When to run

- A significant Printing Press upgrade (new MCP surface, new auth modes, new
  transport, scoring rubric changes) would lift this CLI more than manual
  polish.
- The published CLI ships with a known systemic gap a reprint would fix.
- The user wants prior novel features re-evaluated against the current
  machine and current personas, not carried forward verbatim.

For one-off code-quality fixes, prefer `/printing-press-polish` — it doesn't
redo research or rebuild the manuscript.

## Setup

```bash
PRESS_HOME="${PRINTING_PRESS_HOME:-$HOME/printing-press}"
PRESS_LIBRARY="$PRESS_HOME/library"
PRESS_MANUSCRIPTS="$PRESS_HOME/manuscripts"

# Mid-pipeline callers may pass printing_press_bin: <abs-path> in the args
# bundle. Prefer it so reprint keeps using the parent skill's preflight-selected
# binary instead of re-resolving through PATH.
PRINTING_PRESS_BIN="${PRINTING_PRESS_BIN:-}"
if [ -z "$PRINTING_PRESS_BIN" ] && [ -n "${ARGUMENTS:-}" ]; then
  PRINTING_PRESS_BIN="$(printf '%s\n' "catapult-openfield-connect and zotero-research-library pp-clis lost in machine migration" | sed -nE 's/^[[:space:]]*printing_press_bin:[[:space:]]*(.+)$/\1/p' | head -1)"
fi
if [ -z "$PRINTING_PRESS_BIN" ]; then
  PRINTING_PRESS_BIN="$(command -v cli-printing-press 2>/dev/null || true)"
fi

if [ -z "$PRINTING_PRESS_BIN" ]; then
  echo "cli-printing-press binary not found."
  echo "Install with:  go install github.com/mvanhorn/cli-printing-press/v4/cmd/cli-printing-press@latest"
  return 1 2>/dev/null || exit 1
fi
echo "PRINTING_PRESS_BIN=$PRINTING_PRESS_BIN"
```

## Phase A — Resolve and reconcile presence

Resolve the user's argument the same way `/printing-press-import` does:
fetch the public library `registry.json` once, then exact → normalized →
fuzzy match. The argument can be an API slug (`notion`), a brand name
(`cal.com`), an old `<api>-pp-cli` form, or close enough.

Capture from the matched registry entry: `API_SLUG` (from `.name`) and
`LIB_PATH` (from `.path`, e.g., `library/productivity/cal-com`). Phase B
uses `$LIB_PATH` for the public patches fetch. For the "present | absent"
never-published row, `$LIB_PATH` stays empty — Phase B's fetch
short-circuits on that.

Then check what exists locally and reconcile against the public library by
reading both provenance manifests' `run_id` and `generated_at`:

| Local | Public registry | Action |
|-------|-----------------|--------|
| absent | absent | STOP — nothing to reprint; suggest `/printing-press <api>` for a fresh print |
| absent | present | invoke `/printing-press-import <api>`, then continue |
| present | absent | continue — never-published local CLI; skip import |
| present, same `run_id` | present | continue without import |
| present, public newer `generated_at` | present | offer import via `AskUserQuestion`; user decides |
| present, local newer `generated_at` | present | STOP — local has unpublished work; tell user to publish or discard first |

When invoking `/printing-press-import`, let it own backup, overwrite,
build-verify, and module-path-rewrite. Wait for it to return clean before
continuing.

## Phase B — Verify reconcilable prior context

Locate the two artifacts the writing pipeline should be aware of: research
(drives novel-features Pass 2(d)) and patches (post-publish hand-fixes
recorded by `/printing-press-amend`, e.g. live-discovered API quirks the
spec didn't reveal).

```bash
LIB_TARGET="$PRESS_LIBRARY/$API_SLUG"
LIB_RESEARCH="$LIB_TARGET/research.json"
MAN_RESEARCH=$(ls -1t "$PRESS_MANUSCRIPTS/$API_SLUG"/*/research.json 2>/dev/null | head -1)
```

### Research absent

If neither research path exists, the published CLI predates `research.json`
provenance. The subagent will treat the run as a first print and Pass 2(d)
reprint reconciliation will not fire — there is nothing for it to read.
Surface this and ask:

> Published `<api>` was built before `research.json` provenance landed.
> Without it, the novel-features subagent will treat this as a first
> print — there is nothing to reconcile against. Continue as a degraded
> reprint (essentially a fresh print with a kept binary name)?

If the user declines, exit. If they continue, record the absence so the
hand-off prompt notes that this is a degraded reprint.

### Patches discovery

Refresh the local patches index from public when reachable, then read
locally so downstream references are durable. Amends may have landed
against the public copy without triggering a regen, so the local copy
can lag even when `run_id` matches; this step closes that gap.

The index ships in one of two shapes: the per-patch directory
`.printing-press-patches/` (current) or the legacy single-array
`.printing-press-patches.json` (older CLIs not yet normalized). Always check
both shapes when reachable. Prefer the directory when it contains patch files,
but never let an absent legacy single-file index set `PATCH_COUNT=0` until the
directory fallback has been read.

```bash
PATCHES_DIR="$LIB_TARGET/.printing-press-patches"
PATCHES_LEGACY="$LIB_TARGET/.printing-press-patches.json"
if [[ -n "$LIB_PATH" ]]; then
  # Fetch the legacy shape if present, but do not treat a 404 as proof that no
  # patches exist. Current library entries may carry only the per-patch
  # directory below.
  tmp=$(mktemp)
  if gh api -H "Accept: application/vnd.github.v3.raw" \
       "repos/mvanhorn/printing-press-library/contents/$LIB_PATH/.printing-press-patches.json" \
       > "$tmp" 2>/dev/null; then
    mv "$tmp" "$PATCHES_LEGACY"
  else
    rm -f "$tmp"
  fi

  # Fetch the current directory shape independently. This is the required
  # fallback when `.printing-press-patches.json` is absent.
  listing=$(gh api "repos/mvanhorn/printing-press-library/contents/$LIB_PATH/.printing-press-patches" 2>/dev/null || true)
  if jq -e 'type == "array"' <<<"$listing" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    mkdir -p "$PATCHES_DIR"
    jq -r '.[] | select(.name | endswith(".json")) | "\(.name)\t\(.download_url)"' <<<"$listing" \
    | while IFS=$'\t' read -r name url; do
        tmp=$(mktemp)
        if curl -fsSL "$url" -o "$tmp" 2>/dev/null; then
          mv "$tmp" "$PATCHES_DIR/$name"   # atomic: a dropped transfer never leaves corrupt JSON
        else
          rm -f "$tmp"
        fi
      done
  fi
fi

# Count from the first non-empty shape locally; PATCHES_SOURCE is what Phase D reads.
if [[ -d "$PATCHES_DIR" ]]; then
  DIR_PATCH_COUNT=$(find "$PATCHES_DIR" -maxdepth 1 -name '*.json' ! -name '_meta.json' | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
else
  DIR_PATCH_COUNT=0
fi
if [[ "$DIR_PATCH_COUNT" != "0" ]]; then
  PATCH_COUNT="$DIR_PATCH_COUNT"
  PATCHES_SOURCE="$PATCHES_DIR"
elif [[ -f "$PATCHES_LEGACY" ]]; then
  PATCH_COUNT=$(jq '(.patches // []) | length' "$PATCHES_LEGACY" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
  PATCHES_SOURCE="$PATCHES_LEGACY"
else
  PATCH_COUNT=0
  PATCHES_SOURCE="$PATCHES_DIR"
fi
```

If `$PATCH_COUNT == 0` or no index is present (older CLI predating the
patches contract), skip the rest of this subsection — no patches block in
the hand-off.

If `$PATCH_COUNT > 0`, surface a one-liner to the user before continuing:

> Public `<api>` has `$PATCH_COUNT` recorded patch(es) against the prior
> printed CLI. Will carry into the brief as a watch-list (informational,
> not a re-apply mandate) so the fresh code doesn't silently regress
> live-validated fixes.

Hold `$PATCHES_SOURCE` and `$PATCH_COUNT` for Phase D.

## Phase C — Recency recommendation

Pull `researched_at` from the most-recent prior `research.json` and
`printing_press_version` + `generated_at` from `.printing-press.json`:

```bash
RESEARCHED_AT=$(jq -r '.researched_at // empty' "$MAN_RESEARCH" 2>/dev/null)
PRESS_VERSION=$(jq -r '.printing_press_version // empty' "$LIB_TARGET/.printing-press.json" 2>/dev/null)
GENERATED_AT=$(jq -r '.generated_at // empty' "$LIB_TARGET/.printing-press.json" 2>/dev/null)
```

Compute the calendar age of the research with `python3` so it stays portable
across macOS/Linux and tolerates the microsecond precision that
`generated_at` carries (BSD `date -f` rejects fractional seconds; `python3`
is on every supported platform):

```bash
AGE_DAYS=$(python3 -c "
from datetime import datetime, timezone
ts = '$RESEARCHED_AT'.replace('Z', '+00:00')
print(int((datetime.now(timezone.utc) - datetime.fromisoformat(ts)).total_seconds() // 86400))
" 2>/dev/null)
```

Surface both signals to the user — research age and prior machine version.
Age thresholds are rules of thumb, not gates:

- under 30 days → reuse looks safe
- 30–120 days → reuse plausible; the user should mention any known API
  churn in their reprint reason so the subagent's Pass 2 picks it up
- over 120 days → redo recommended

Don't predict API churn from age alone — describe the signals and let the
user override. The Phase 0 binary-version-bump revalidation in
`/printing-press` handles the machine-delta side independently; don't
duplicate it here.

Ask via `AskUserQuestion`:

1. **Reuse prior research** — keep the prior brief; the subagent re-scores
   prior novel features against current personas
2. **Redo research** — re-run Phase 1 from scratch; the subagent still
   ingests prior novel features as Pass 2(d) input
3. **Show me first** — display the prior brief's headline + novel-features
   list, then re-ask between options 1 and 2

## Phase D — Hand off to `/printing-press`

Before invoking `/printing-press`, use the prior CLI's scorecard and manifest
to decide whether the reprint should offer spec enrichment that the first print
could not have used. Reprints have better evidence than fresh prints: they know
which structural dimensions were weak, which Printing Press version produced
the prior CLI, and what the user named as the reason for regenerating.

Find the most recent scorecard JSON from the prior manuscript run. If no
scorecard artifact exists, run a fresh structural scorecard against the local
library copy:

```bash
SCORECARD_SOURCE=$(ls -1t "$PRESS_MANUSCRIPTS/$API_SLUG"/*/proofs/scorecard.json 2>/dev/null | head -1)
SCORECARD_JSON=""
if [[ -n "$SCORECARD_SOURCE" ]]; then
  SCORECARD_JSON=$(cat "$SCORECARD_SOURCE" 2>/dev/null || true)
elif [[ -d "$LIB_TARGET" ]]; then
  SCORECARD_SOURCE=$(mktemp)
  if "$PRINTING_PRESS_BIN" scorecard --dir "$LIB_TARGET" --json > "$SCORECARD_SOURCE" 2>/dev/null; then
    SCORECARD_JSON=$(cat "$SCORECARD_SOURCE" 2>/dev/null || true)
  fi
  rm -f "$SCORECARD_SOURCE"
  SCORECARD_SOURCE=""
fi
```

If `SCORECARD_JSON` is empty, continue without enrichment prompting and say the
reprint is proceeding without prior score evidence. Do not invent a prompt from
the reprint reason alone.

When `SCORECARD_JSON` is available, inspect only dimensions that map to a
pre-generation spec edit and skip dimensions that already score 10/10:

- `mcp_remote_transport`, `mcp_token_efficiency`, `mcp_tool_design`, and
  `mcp_surface_strategy` below 10 can be lifted by the `/printing-press`
  Phase 2 section **Pre-Generation MCP Enrichment**. Examples:
  - remote transport is below 10: offer `mcp.transport: [stdio, http]` or the
    OpenAPI `x-mcp.transport` equivalent before regeneration.
  - token efficiency, tool design, or surface strategy is below 10: offer the
    Phase 2 MCP surface decision, including intents for clear multi-step
    workflows or the Cloudflare pattern for large surfaces.
- `auth_protocol` below 10, or prior manifest evidence that the CLI used a
  slug-derived env var where the ecosystem has a canonical env var, can be
  lifted by **Pre-Generation Auth Enrichment**. Offer to carry canonical
  `auth.env_vars` or OpenAPI `x-auth-env-vars` guidance into the spec.
- `data_pipeline_integrity` below 10 is only an enrichment opportunity when the
  prior CLI or research shows sync-eligible resources. In that case, point the
  handoff at the relevant Phase 2 sync/cache enrichment decision rather than
  treating the score alone as proof that a local store should exist.

Use `AskUserQuestion` for each concrete opportunity before the handoff. Phrase
the question around the scorecard evidence and the named canonical section, not
around a freeform rewrite. Example:

> Prior scorecard shows `mcp_remote_transport: 5/10`. Offer MCP transport
> enrichment before regenerating, using `/printing-press` Phase 2
> **Pre-Generation MCP Enrichment** as the source of truth?

Options:

1. **Apply enrichment to the handoff** - include the selected spec edit in the
   `/printing-press` prompt so Phase 2 can update the spec before generation.
2. **Skip for this reprint** - leave the spec unchanged for this dimension.
3. **Show score evidence first** - print the relevant scorecard lines and then
   re-ask between options 1 and 2.

Do not auto-apply enrichment. If the prior scorecard already has
`mcp_remote_transport: 10/10`, do not ask the redundant MCP transport question.
If the user accepts any opportunity, add a `## Reprint Spec Enrichment`
section to the `/printing-press` handoff. Keep it brief: name the weak
dimension, the accepted enrichment, and the canonical `/printing-press` Phase 2
section to execute. Do not duplicate the canonical enrichment text here.

Invoke `/printing-press <api>` and bundle these into the prompt:

1. **A header line** stating the user already chose to regenerate, so
   Phase 0's library-check should select "Generate a fresh CLI" and not
   re-prompt fresh-vs-improve.
2. **Research mode** from Phase C (`reuse` or `redo`). Phase 0's existing
   reuse logic consumes this.
3. **The user's freeform reprint reason**, verbatim, in a `User context`
   block. This propagates into the brief as `## User Vision` and becomes
   Pass 2(e) input to the novel-features subagent — the right hook for
   "I want better MCP support" → bias the brainstorm accordingly.
4. **Reprint spec enrichment** — only when the scorecard-driven prompt above
   found an accepted opportunity. Include under a
   `## Reprint Spec Enrichment` heading.
5. **Prior patches** — only when Phase B found `$PATCH_COUNT > 0`.
   Include under a `## Prior Patches` heading.

   Lead the section with this framing sentence, verbatim:

   > The following were hand-fixed against the prior printed CLI. They
   > are informational — the machine may have absorbed some of these
   > upstream since the patch was applied. Stay aware so the fresh code
   > doesn't silently regress the underlying API truth or architectural
   > pattern, but do not treat as a re-apply checklist.

   Then summarize the patches from `$PATCHES_SOURCE`. Lead each entry
   with the *substance* the patch encodes (the API truth, the
   architectural pattern, the cross-file convention) drawn from each
   patch's `reason` and `validated_outcome` — not just `summary`. Patch
   metadata (`id`, `files`) is fine as parenthetical context but never
   the headline.

   Scale the section to patch count:

   - **1–3 patches**: one short paragraph per patch — substance first,
     then how it manifested. Model the shape on:
     > Linear's personal API keys go in `Authorization: lin_api_…` raw,
     > with no `Bearer` prefix; OAuth tokens use `Authorization: Bearer
     > <token>`. The prior CLI shipped with `auth set-token` only
     > (Bearer-defaulted) and was patched post-publish to add
     > `auth set-api-key` plus the raw-header path in `config.go`
     > (`linear-auth-api-key-vs-oauth-token`).
   - **4–9 patches**: one tight sentence per patch, same substance-first
     shape.
   - **10+ patches**: thematic summary by category (auth, pagination,
     query encoding, MCP additions, helpers, classifiers, error
     envelopes). Two or three sentences per theme citing 2–3 patch `id`s
     as evidence. Do not enumerate all entries inline.

   Close the section with a pointer so a downstream agent can drill into
   any specific patch when working in the relevant area:

   > Full patch detail: the per-patch files under `$PATCHES_SOURCE`
   > (each `<id>.json` is one self-contained patch; the legacy
   > single-array `.printing-press-patches.json` carries the same fields
   > under `patches[]`).

Do **not** pass a separate "this is a reprint" marker. The novel-features
subagent runs unconditionally on every print and discovers prior research
via its own discovery snippet (see
`skills/printing-press/references/novel-features-subagent.md`). The paths
import populated in Phase A are exactly the paths it checks; Pass 2(d)
fires whenever prior `research.json` exists.

The library-preservation contract is owned by `/printing-press` Phase 5.6
("Promote to Library"), not by this skill. When the existing library has
`novel_features > 0` in its manifest (or hand-authored files under
`internal/cli/`, `internal/syncer/`, or `internal/store/`), Phase 5.6 first
dry-runs `"$PRINTING_PRESS_BIN" regen-merge "$LIB_TARGET" --fresh "$CLI_WORK_DIR"
--json` to decide whether the fresh tree rebuilt the prior novels. If the
fresh tree contains all prior novel work, Phase 5.6 uses the swap path and
treats generated-file version drift as expected overwrite. Otherwise it routes
promotion through `regen-merge --apply` so still-unique hand-authored novels
survive the reprint and genuine `NOVEL-COLLISION` / missing-referent cases halt
for review. This honors the prefer-`regen-merge` guidance under the
**Hand-edits must be regen-mergeable.** section of
`skills/printing-press/SKILL.md` (anchor `hand-edit-durability`). If a future
edit to that phase changes the routing rule, update this paragraph in the same
PR -- the reprint skill is the dominant entry point that fires it.

Before the hand-off, compare regenerated manifest files against the tracked
published tree. If `$LIB_TARGET/manifest.json` or
`$LIB_TARGET/tools-manifest.json` exists, diff each file against the freshly
generated counterpart under `$CLI_WORK_DIR` and surface non-empty diffs in the
handoff prompt. Treat a diff as a reconciliation checkpoint, not as automatic
overwrite approval: the operator must decide whether to preserve the tracked
hand-edit, fold it into the spec/research inputs, or intentionally accept the
regenerated value. Do not continue silently when tracked manifest fields,
tool metadata, or descriptions would be dropped.

Attribution also stays owned by `/printing-press`: the hand-off runs generation
for the same API slug, and the generate/promote path must preserve the existing
library manifest's permanent `creator` while adding the reprinter to
`contributors[]` when they differ. Do not repair this by hand-editing
`creator`, `contributors[]`, README bylines, SKILL `author:`, or NOTICE; rerun
with a current Printing Press binary so the manifest-first guard rewrites the
working tree and promoted tree consistently.

## After hand-off

The printing-press flow drives the rest. Don't summarize its work — let
the user see the live phases.

If `/printing-press` halts with the subagent's pre-flight HALT (brief
lacks concrete `Users` / `Top Workflows` content), the reused prior brief
predates the subagent's required schema. Recommend re-running with **Redo
research** selected at Phase C.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/cli-printing-press/skills/printing-press

# /printing-press

Generate the best useful CLI for an API without burning an hour on phase theater.

```bash
/printing-press Notion
/printing-press Discord codex
/printing-press --spec ./openapi.yaml
/printing-press --har ./capture.har --name MyAPI
/printing-press https://postman.com/explore
/printing-press https://postman.com
```

## What Changed In v2

The old skill inflated the path to ship:
- too many mandatory research documents before code existed
- too many separate late-stage validation phases after code existed
- too many chances to discover obvious failures late

This version uses one lean loop:
1. Resolve the spec and write one research brief
2. Generate
3. Build the highest-value gaps
4. Run one shipcheck block
5. Optionally run live API smoke tests

Artifacts are still written, but only the ones that materially help the next step.

## Modes

### Default

Normal mode. Claude does research, generation orchestration, implementation, and verification.

### Codex Mode

If the arguments include `codex` or `--codex`, offload pure code-writing tasks to Codex CLI.

Use Codex for:
- writing store/data-layer code
- writing workflow commands
- fixing dead flags / dead code / path issues
- README cookbook edits

Keep on Claude:
- research and product positioning
- choosing which gaps matter
- verification results and ship decisions

If Codex fails 3 times in a row, stop delegating and finish locally.

### Polish Mode (Standalone Skill)

For second-pass improvements to an existing CLI, use the standalone polish skill:

```bash
/printing-press-polish redfin
```

See the `printing-press-polish` skill for details. It runs diagnostics, fixes verify failures, removes dead code, cleans up descriptions and README, and offers to publish.

## Rules

- **Do not ship a CLI that hasn't been behaviorally tested against real targets.** `go build` and `verify` pass-rate are structural signals, not correctness signals. Phase 5's mechanical test matrix runs every subcommand + `--json` + error paths; if that matrix was not executed, the CLI is not shippable. Quick Check is the floor; Full Dogfood is required when the user asks for thoroughness.
- **Bugs found during dogfood are fix-before-ship, not "file for v0.2".** If a 1-3 file edit resolves it, do it now. `ship-with-gaps` is deprecated as a default verdict (see Phase 4). Context is freshest in-session; a v0.2 backlog that may never be revisited ships known-broken CLIs.
- **Features approved in Phase 1.5 are shipping scope.** Do not downgrade a shipping-scope feature to a stub mid-build. If implementation becomes infeasible, return to Phase 1.5 with a revised manifest and get explicit re-approval.
- **Do not quote human-time estimates for sub-tasks** ("~15-30 min", "~1 hour", "quick fix") in `AskUserQuestion` options, phase descriptions, or reference docs. The agent does the work, not the user; agent-fabricated estimates are notoriously bad and train users to distrust the prompt. Describe scope instead (lines of code, files touched, relative size). The carve-outs are wall-clock estimates for genuinely time-bound things: the whole-CLI run (set the user's expectation up front — most CLIs take 30+ minutes), tool installs (`go install` takes ~10 seconds), and printing-press subcommands that do network-bound work (crowd-sniff scans npm + GitHub, ~5-10 minutes). Anything bounded by agent reasoning time is not time-bound — describe scope.
- **Use raw captures for contract research.** When reading official docs, auth/error/rate-limit pages, endpoint references, OpenAPI/Postman links, or source pages whose exact identifiers affect the generated CLI, read [references/fetch-docs.md](references/fetch-docs.md) and use its `fetch-docs.sh` helper. Reserve `WebFetch` for quick TL;DR reads where losing field-level details is acceptable.
- Optimize for time-to-ship, not time-to-document.
- Reuse prior research whenever it is already good enough.
- Do not split one idea across multiple mandatory artifacts.
- Durable files produced by this skill go under `$PRESS_RUNSTATE/` (working state) or `$PRESS_MANUSCRIPTS/` (archived). Short-lived command captures may use `/tmp/printing-press/` and must be removed after use.
- Do not create a separate narrative phase for dogfood, dead-code audit, runtime verification, and final score. Treat them as one shipcheck block.
- Run cheap, high-signal checks early.
- Fix blockers and high-leverage failures first.
- Reuse the same spec path across `generate`, `dogfood`, `verify`, and `scorecard`.
- YAML, JSON, local paths, and URLs are all valid spec inputs for the verification tools.
- Maximum 2 verification fix loops unless the user explicitly asks for more.

## Secret & PII Protection (Cardinal Rules)

**These rules are non-negotiable. They apply at ALL times during a run.**

API key **values**, token **values**, passwords, and session cookies must NEVER
appear in any artifact: source code, manuscripts, proofs, READMEs, HARs, or
anything committed to git. Env var **names** (e.g., `STEAM_API_KEY`) and
placeholders (e.g., `"your-key-here"`) are safe.

During Phase 5.6 (archiving) and before publishing, read and apply
